catalog_quote: THE ACCENT. 1. On the whole the accent in Balochi is less strongly marked than in English. 2. All long vowels are accented : e.g., sarbar, a load, bale; sidha, straight; madhagh, a female. 3. [scanned '8.'] In words containing more than one long vowel the last receives the stronger accent : e.g., mdtiun, a stepmother; mdzath, a two-year-old camel; holpish, armour. 4. Diphthongs are accented in the same way as long vowels ... 5. Quiescent letters, letters not followed by a vowel, are accented : e.g., ikhtar, so much; chukhchort, children; shamnam, dew. 6. It follows therefore that compound letters, letters under the sign shadda, are accented : e.g., baqgal, a grocer; duggaz, the lammergeier; shakk, doubt. ... 7. In the case of short vowels the first should be slightly accented : e.g., birinj, husked rice; philkand, sugar; kharagh, a bank. 8. In words containing three short vowels th…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Gilbertson 1925 'The Accent' passage is verbatim in the djvu text we hold at the stated place (Appendix I, between dictionary p.793 and the 'APPENDIX II 799' running head, i.e. p.797 as cited by Korn and Jahani & Korn), and the Jahani & Korn 2009 secondary quote is verbatim on chapter p.649. (2) Deciding source: a 1925 colonial dictionary appendix (impressionistic, one page), but the two specialist treatments we also hold -- Korn 2003/2005 pp.67-70 and Jahani & Korn 2009 sec. 2.2.1 -- explicitly say this is essentially all that exists for Eastern Balochi stress and interpret it exactly as our record does (weight-sensitive, last heavy syllable; prefixes/complex verbs one accent unit; all-light words initial, three-light first+third). Korn additionally flags Gilbertson's internal inconsistencies (birinj/philkand initial accent despite final cluster; phirishtagh)

tone.quote: This variety of EHB differs greatly from dialects 1-3 and is quite incomprehensible to them, mainly because of its development of a strong stress-accent, whereby unstressed vowels are lost, and the resulting consonant clusters give rise to complex assimilations and dissimilations. Final vowels are everywhere dropped as well, resulting in far-reaching morphological changes.
tone.locator: p. 97, 'The dialects of EHB', no. 4 (the Kasrani subdialect)

sources.note: Second-hand (Syed, Shah, Xu & Xu 2022: 8-9, citing 'Elfenbein 1997a'): it describes Balochi word prosody as stress falling on a long vowel or diphthong, with no contrastive lexical stress; Balochi is treated throughout the literature as a stress-accent language, so any tone remark here would be a 'no lexical tone' statement. The only dedicated modern phonology chapter for Balochi as a whole and not previously listed here.

tone.quote: The Balochi accent remains an issue to be investigated. Most studies on Balochi and collections of Balochi texts have neglected it altogether. [...] Information on the accent in the Eastern dialects is even harder to find than for the others. The description by GILBERTSON 1925/II:797, although set in categories different from those used here, seems to indicate rules very much like (if not identical with) those observed for Karachi Balochi, i.e. the last heavy syllable of a word being accented.
tone.locator: ch. II 1.3 'Accent', p. 67 (opening) and p. 69 (Eastern dialects paragraph) of the HAL
